sections.h2: How do you sell a house fast in Bloomfield, NJ?
sections.html:
The quickest Bloomfield sales are ones where the seller has the township paperwork moving before a buyer is found. Whether you list, sell privately or accept a cash offer, the Township's Transfer of Property Title inspection has to be passed, and its application is due 30 days before closing.

Listing makes sense for a house that shows well and a seller who can handle repair requests. A cash offer fits a house with a long punch list, a two or three family with tenants, a property carrying open permits, or an inherited home where heirs want a single closing. Half of Bloomfield's homes are rented, so many owners here are landlords weighing a sale against another year of upkeep.

  • Traditional listing: broad buyer pool, commission, inspections and a lender's timeline.
  • Private sale: no listing commission, more of the paperwork on you.
  • Cash buyer: as-is purchase, shorter timeline, price reduced for the repairs the buyer takes on.

sections.h2: What kind of town is Bloomfield, New Jersey?
sections.html:
Bloomfield is a compact Essex County township of 5.34 square miles of land, home to a July 2025 Census estimate of 56,375 residents, up 6.2 percent from the 2020 base. Density was 9,950.3 people per square mile in 2020. The township borders Belleville, East Orange, Glen Ridge, Montclair, Newark and Nutley in Essex County and Clifton in Passaic County, and it includes the Brookdale and Watsessing neighborhoods plus a slice of Silver Lake.

Only 50.7 percent of housing units are owner-occupied, so Bloomfield is a half-renter town. For 2020 to 2024 the median owner-occupied home was valued at $470,800, median household income was $103,604, and median gross rent was $1,824. Foreign-born residents make up 25.1 percent of the population, 30.9 percent of residents identify as Hispanic or Latino, and 35.0 percent of people age 5 and older speak a language other than English at home.

The land was first patented to colonists from Newark and assigned to Essex County in 1675. The Presbyterian Society of Bloomfield formed in 1794, and the township's population jumped from 9,668 in 1900 to 38,077 in 1930, which points to an older housing stock and a long paper trail of permits.

sections.h2: What is the Transfer of Property Title in Bloomfield?
sections.html:
It is the Township's required inspection and certificate for any sale or transfer of property. The application is due 30 days before the closing date, and the certificate stays valid for six months. The Fire Department handles it from 375 Franklin Street, and the application form says the inspection also serves as the state smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certificate.

The form states that the inspection shows only that a general check of the visible parts of the building found no code violations or unsafe conditions at that time. The township's FAQ adds that if a bank insists on a separate certificate, the Fire Prevention Bureau issues one for $35, although state law allows a single certificate.

sections.h2: What does the Bloomfield inspector check?
sections.html:
The Township publishes a checklist that is not exhaustive, so the inspector can ask for more. Most items are practical repairs a seller can finish in a weekend, but a few take weeks, such as closing old permits and replacing a lead service line.

  • All construction permits, past and present, closed with final inspections.
  • Proof that any lead or galvanized water service line on private property has been replaced, documented by a New Jersey plumber.
  • A township-approved water meter in place, even if the building is winterized.
  • Sump pumps and downspouts not tied into the sanitary sewer.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors on each floor and near bedrooms, 10-year sealed battery or hard-wired.
  • A fire-rated, self-closing door between an attached garage and the house.
  • Handrails on stairs with four or more risers, no loose siding or roofing, and numbered units.
  • No unregistered vehicles, debris or trip hazards on the property.

Three-family and larger buildings also need portable fire extinguishers, mounted near an exit within 10 feet of the kitchen. If the new owner will rent the property, the form says the rental must be registered within six months of closing.

sections.h2: Do oil tanks and basement apartments cause problems in Bloomfield?
sections.html:
They can. The township's fire FAQ says an unused oil tank must be removed or abandoned in place within one year, and either path needs a Fire Sub-Code permit from the Building Department. If a tank was removed with a permit, the Fire Department or Building Department may have the paperwork on file, so call the Fire Prevention Bureau before you hunt for records.

Basement apartments are a larger issue. The FAQ states that most are illegal, especially in three-family houses, because they do not meet egress requirements. Check with the Building Inspector before you advertise one as a rental unit, because an unpermitted unit can stall a Transfer of Property Title and spook a lender.

sections.h2: How are Bloomfield property taxes billed and appealed?
sections.html:
Quarterly taxes are due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1, and interest starts ten calendar days after the due date. A lost or missing bill does not excuse a payment, since N.J.S.A. 54:4-64 says failure to receive a bill does not invalidate the tax. If you just bought or are selling, call the Tax Collector for the amount due and a copy of the bill.

The Tax Assessor handles assessments, deductions for senior citizens, disabled persons and veterans, and appeals. An appeal is due by April 1 of the tax year, or by May 1 in a year when a revaluation or reassessment takes effect. State relief programs listed by the township include the Homestead Rebate, NJSAVER, the Property Tax Deduction or Credit and Property Tax Reimbursement, so an owner receiving one should tell the closing attorney.

The Tax Assessor's Office is at 1 Municipal Plaza, first floor, Room 108, and the Tax Collector accepts payments from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. in person or online.

sections.h2: What do trains, highways and schools add to Bloomfield listings?
sections.html:
The Garden State Parkway has four interchanges in the township, numbered 148 through 151, with 148 and 151 complete and 149 and 150 partial. The Essex toll plaza sits southbound just south of interchange 150. County Road 506, its spur and County Road 509 also cross the township, and Bloomfield has 95.39 miles of roadway in all.

South Bloomfield is served by two NJ Transit Montclair-Boonton Line stations, one off Bloomfield Avenue downtown and one at Watsessing Avenue and Orange Street. About 55 percent of weekday trains continue to New York Penn Station, and weekend trains end at Hoboken. Mean travel time to work is 32.4 minutes. Bloomfield Public Schools run 11 schools and enrolled 6,191 students in 2021 to 2022, from pre-kindergarten through Bloomfield High School and Bridges Academy. Bloomfield Tech High School is a countywide magnet school.

sections.h2: When is a cash sale worth considering in Bloomfield?
sections.html:
A cash sale is worth a look when a Transfer of Property Title would take longer than you can wait, or when repairs would cost more than the buyer discount. Ask any cash buyer to put in writing who orders the inspection, who pays the fee and who replaces a lead service line if one turns up.

For an estate, remember the state treats an executor's sale to an outside buyer as a taxable transfer for the realty transfer fee, while a transfer to a named heir is exempt. Compare the net on each path and have a New Jersey attorney review the contract.

faqs.q: Is a smoke detector certificate separate from the Bloomfield Transfer of Property Title?
faqs.a: Usually not. The township's application form says the Transfer of Property Title inspection also serves as the smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate. A separate certificate from the Fire Prevention Bureau costs $35 if your bank refuses the single one.

faqs.q: How long before closing should I apply for a Transfer of Property Title in Bloomfield?
faqs.a: 30 days. The township's form says the application must be submitted 30 days prior to the closing date, and the certificate is valid for six months. Reinspection after a failed visit costs $25.

faqs.q: Do I have to replace a lead water line to sell in Bloomfield?
faqs.a: Yes, if the service line on your property is lead or galvanized. The township says the owner must replace it and show proof before a Transfer of Property Title is issued. A New Jersey licensed plumber must inspect and document the line's material.

faqs.q: What is the property tax appeal deadline in Bloomfield?
faqs.a: April 1 of the tax year. In a year when a revaluation or reassessment takes effect, the deadline moves to May 1. Ask the Tax Assessor's Office for the forms.

faqs.q: Is a sale to a family member exempt from the New Jersey realty transfer fee?
faqs.a: A sale between parent and child is exempt, including an adopted child. A stepchild does not qualify, so a parent selling to a stepchild owes the fee unless the child was legally adopted.
